title: Prompted, or Not
aliases: A Town That Lasts One Day
logline: Two selling strips on two low-country roads: at one an arm goes out at the verge and a vehicle stops because it was hailed, at the other the road is so buried in fruit for eight weeks that vehicles slow with nobody signalling to them at all — and from ten metres away, through a long lens, there is no telling which is which.
human_question: When I reach for something, how much of the reaching was mine — and would anybody watching me, including me, be able to tell the difference?

place.what_kind_of_place: Two stretches of road where one trade occupies both verges and nothing else does, an hour or so apart in the same low country, and deliberately unlike each other in every way except that. The first is a straight stretch of an old trunk road, the island's main inland artery, where several dozen households sell one nut all year round: stalls shoulder to shoulder facing the traffic, some still frames of poles under coconut-leaf thatch and some small fronts of block and tin, the goods sealed in packets from the size of a matchbox upward, raw, roasted, salted and spiced, and not grown anywhere near the road they are sold on. The second is a through road in a river valley where a fruit tree introduced centuries ago grows in back gardens and over lanes rather than in plantations, so that for eight or nine weeks a year the verge fills with temporary stalls of poles, wire and tarpaulin heaped with the same red fruit, and for the other forty-four weeks it is a road with houses along it and nothing to stop for. On both, the selling is done standing at the edge of the tarmac, and the market is whatever is coming round the bend at sixty kilometres an hour.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: This is the group's fast film and it is built out of one repeated unit: six seconds, from an arm going out to a vehicle rejoining the traffic. It is shot almost entirely on long lenses from the far side of a carriageway, which compresses two rows of stalls and a stream of traffic into a single shallow plane where everything is happening at once and nothing can be resolved — the honest optical version of what the film is about. Three things carry it with the sound off. The rate: forty or fifty approaches an hour on one verge, the refusals hugely outnumbering the sales, cut at the speed they happen until the pattern rather than any transaction is what you are watching. The colour and sound of two completely different roads doing the same thing, one all sealed packets and dust and diesel in flat midday glare, the other a two-kilometre red line under wet tarpaulin in the last hour of light, with the traffic noise never once dropping out. And the thing the whole film is built to earn, which is a cut rather than a shot: the same lens, the same height, the same distance across the same width of road, one vehicle stopping because somebody stepped out and hailed it and one stopping because it slowed on its own, laid end to end so that a viewer tries to tell them apart and cannot. There is no aerial reveal and no golden-hour payoff in this film. If a drone goes up at all it is flat and overhead and used as a diagram — a road and a pattern of braking — for a few seconds, and never as a flourish.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Traffic, and two different clocks. The trunk-road strip runs on a day: shutters up before six and shelves laid out in the dark against a road that is still mostly lorries, a working morning when almost nothing stops, an afternoon and a weekend when up-country traffic multiplies the stopping rate and the arms are out continuously, then stock carried in and shutters down and a road that is only a road again. The valley road runs on a season, and a glut has its own shape: very little fruit and an absurd price in the first week, more of it by the peak than the road can absorb with the chalked price rewritten lower, and a last week in which the stalls come down faster than they went up. Rain empties either verge in four minutes and fills it again in ten. Cutting the two clocks against each other — a day against a season, a permanent trade against an eight-week one — is how the film gets its structure without a single slow move in it.
place.when_it_looks_best: Daylight and dry weather, because the whole trade happens standing outdoors on a shoulder. The trunk-road strip wants two contrasting days rather than one: an ordinary working weekday, when almost nothing stops, and a weekend or holiday afternoon, when the same hundred metres behaves like a different place. The valley road exists as a subject only inside its eight or nine weeks, roughly late May to the middle of August, heaviest through June and July, and its first and last weeks are worth as much as its peak. First light for the laying-out on both; the last two hours of light for the arms against low sun, the lamps coming on over the tarpaulins and the shutters coming down. The film does not wait for beautiful light and does not end on any.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A fast, compressed piece about a kind of work almost nobody has filmed at the speed it actually runs: a livelihood made of interrupting strangers who are on their way somewhere else, where the ordinary result of a morning is a great many people not stopping, and where the whole of a sale — approach, offer, price, note, gone — takes six seconds at the edge of live traffic. Two roads, two crops, two seasons, one economy, cut against each other: an all-year strip of sealed packets on a trunk road and a road that turns red for eight weeks and then stops being a market at all. It has a beginning, a middle and an end without any help — shelves out, shelves in; poles into the verge, poles stacked against a wall — and its payoff is a cut, not a shot. A viewer who never hears a word of narration gets speed, colour, weather, refusal, work and two roads.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes the sources' anatomy of wanting, and specifically the one axis of it that these two roads supply as a filmable pair: whether a state arises by itself or has to be induced. At one strip the inducement is physical and visible — somebody steps out and holds something up. At the other the abundance does the work and vehicles slow unhailed. The voice never contradicts what is on screen, never says anyone is greedy, and points only at what everybody can already see. Then it does the thing the group's whole subject requires: it admits that the distinction it has just drawn is not one the camera can make. We can film which vehicle was hailed. We cannot film which mind was pushed, and neither can anyone standing at the verge. The treatment carries the argument rather than illustrating it — long lens, shallow plane, everything compressed into the same flat distance, two roads that look identical from where the camera has to stand.

sequence.on_screen: Cold open, long lens from the far side of a carriageway on the all-year strip. One complete transaction filling the frame: an arm out at the verge, a windscreen, a window coming down, a packet, a note, the vehicle pulling back into the traffic. Six seconds. Then the same thing again, at a different stall. Then again. Traffic noise at full level throughout, nothing else on the track.
sequence.voice: Everything sold on this road has to be sold to somebody who was not going to stop. That is the whole business, and it takes about six seconds. The old compendiums begin their count of the ordinary mind in exactly this world: the world of what is seen, heard, smelled, tasted and touched.

sequence.on_screen: The same set-up held much longer, and the refusals left in their real proportion: arms going out and windows not coming down, forty or fifty times an hour, nobody at the verge treating it as a defeat. Behind them, shutters going up on another stall and packets being laid out on a shelf.
sequence.voice: The count comes to fifty-four kinds of ordinary mind. Wanting is a large part of it and it is not the whole of it: twenty-four of the fifty-four are the ones these books call beautiful. Nothing along this road is being set up as a trap, and nobody along it is an example of anything.

sequence.on_screen: The cut the film is built on, and the first time the second road appears. Same lens, same height, same distance across the same width of tarmac. A vehicle slows on the all-year strip after somebody steps out and holds a packet up at windscreen height. Cut. On a valley road buried in red fruit, in a different season, a vehicle slows with nobody signalling to it at all and pulls onto the verge. Then both again, alternating, until they stop reading as two places.
sequence.voice: These books set this one force by three dials, and the plainest of them is on the screen now. Wanting either rises sharply, of its own nature, needing nobody — or it has to be urged along, by another person, or by you talking round a part of yourself that was holding back. Two roads. One of these was hailed. The other was not.

sequence.on_screen: The two shots repeated side by side in one frame, matched as exactly as the roads allow, until the eye gives up trying to separate them. Then a slow zoom out to reveal how far away the camera has been standing the whole time: a long lens on a tripod on the opposite shoulder, two rows of stalls flattened into one plane.
sequence.voice: Now the part this film cannot do. From here — from ten metres, from across a road, through a lens — there is no telling which is which. The texts say the urged kind carries a heaviness in it, a sluggishness the sharp kind does not have. That is not a thing a lens can see. We can show you which vehicle was hailed. We cannot show you which mind was pushed, and neither can the person who did the hailing.

sequence.on_screen: A fixed camera on the all-year strip, running long. A vehicle goes past the whole line at speed. A hundred metres on, the brake lights come on. It stops on the shoulder, sits there, then reverses back along the verge to a stall it has already passed. Held in one unbroken shot, at whatever length it really takes.
sequence.voice: And there is the third case, which is the one people recognise in themselves. Nobody urged that. It was urged from the inside, by somebody talking round a mind that was holding back. These books rank that kind weaker than the kind that rises on its own — and they do not, anywhere, say it is therefore somebody else's. Being talked into something makes it smaller in their reckoning. It does not make it not yours.

sequence.on_screen: Faces, but never held and never at the moment money changes hands. Two buyers at one stall on the all-year strip in a single wide frame, one visibly delighted and one showing nothing at all, over the same sealed packet at the same chalked price. Cut to the valley road: a bunch handed through a window, and a picker eating one standing up beside a crate, looking at the traffic, with no expression whatever.
sequence.voice: Underneath the dials there is something simpler. These books say every mind tastes the flavour of whatever it has taken hold of, and that the taste comes three ways and there is no fourth. Then they count: sixty-two kinds of mind carry gladness, fifty-five carry the feeling that is neither one thing nor the other, and the glad kinds of wanting sit squarely among the pleasant ones. Both of those are on this verge right now, over the same packet, for the same price. So a flat face is not evidence of not wanting. And whatever the gladness is, it is not sitting in the packet.

sequence.on_screen: A bargain at a car window in real time, from the arm to the folded note, nobody's words subtitled, the camera far enough away that no face is legible. Then a regular: a vehicle that pulls in unhailed, a packet handed over before anything is said, money already counted, gone in under fifteen seconds.
sequence.voice: Two more things these books say, which this film is going to name and then refuse to use. There is a third dial: whether the wanting arrives carrying a story that excuses it. That lives inside a person, the examples are mostly denials of consequence, and it cannot be read off a stranger through a windscreen — a camera that claims it can has started lying. And one of the two compendiums ranks the flat, unexcited kind of wanting above the glad kind, and gives no reason anywhere we have read. We can show you the flatness. We are not going to tell you what it weighs.

sequence.on_screen: Both endings, cut together and fast. On the valley road, the last week: tarpaulins folded, poles pulled out of the verge and stacked against a wall, wire coiled, and a road with houses along it and nothing to stop for. On the trunk road, the last hour: stock carried in, shutters down one after another, closed boxes and passing headlights. The traffic noise continues over both and is the last thing in the film.
sequence.voice: One thing it would be easy to get backwards. What these books were sorting was never the arm held out over the road. Hospitality and appetite look exactly alike from across a carriageway, and only one of them is being classified. They were describing the moment of reaching, whoever did it and however it arrived. Nobody here was a verdict on anything. Tomorrow the shutters go up again before six, and the other road will be red again in June.

concept_merge.why_together: This record is a merge of two ideas, and the reason is doctrinal rather than editorial. C006 sorts the eight greed-rooted minds on three axes, and one of them is spontaneous or prompted, asaṅkhārika or sasaṅkhārika: whether the state arises sharply and of its own nature [C006-P:L44] or has to be urged on, by another person or by one's own coaxing of a mind that is holding back [C006-M:L5], the urged kind carrying a sluggishness the sharp kind does not [C006-P:L62]. Separately, each of the two absorbed ideas was 'a road where something is sold to people who were not going to stop' — near-duplicates, the same film twice, and neither could do more than assert that axis. Together they give it as a filmable pair on the same kind of ground: at one strip the inducement is a physical, visible, dated invention — somebody steps out and holds something up — and the vehicle stops because it was hailed; at the other the crop is so abundant for eight weeks that vehicles slow on their own, and, as the absorbed idea's own logline had it, from ten metres away there is no telling which is which. That last clause is the film. The distinction is real in the sources, the two strips supply one side of it each, and the camera cannot tell them apart — which is exactly the limit every one of these digests insists on. C004 supplies the frame the axis sits in: the everyday world of what is seen, heard, smelled, tasted and touched [C004-P:L25], greed as the attaching that takes things to be good, beautiful or sweet [C004-M:L13], present with delight in one person and flat routine in another [C004-M:L17], never with displeasure [C004-M:L15], sometimes spontaneous and sometimes because somebody urged it [C004-M:L21], and the count that keeps twenty-four of the fifty-four as beautiful minds [C004-P:L27]. C032 supplies the layer under the dial the camera sees most of: feeling is the tasting of an object's flavour and is in every mind [C032-P:L41] [C032-P:L43], it comes three ways with no fourth [C032-M:L5], and the counts are sixty-two minds carrying gladness and fifty-five carrying neutral feeling [C032-M:L9] [C032-M:L13], with the joyful greed-rooted minds counted squarely among the pleasant ones [C032-P:L58].
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the axis the sources care most about here is the one a camera is worst at. Kept apart, the two films each said 'wanting happens at a roadside' twice, and each would have had to assert the prompted and the spontaneous kinds in the same place, a few metres apart, where the difference is a matter of who moved first. Merged, the film can do something neither could: hold the two sides on two different roads, two different crops and two different seasons, match the shots exactly, and let a viewer fail to sort them. The failure is the finding. It closes off the two cheap endings at the same time. It refuses 'I was talked into it, so it is not mine', because the sources rank prompted wanting weaker without absolving it. And it refuses the idea that the calm buyer is the innocent one, because the same books put neutral feeling in fifty-five kinds of mind including the most refined they know [C032-P:L75–L83], and one of them ranks the flat kind of wanting above the glad kind [C006-M:L19] with no reason the digest could find. What is left is a structure — an arm, a window, six seconds, a price — and a plain statement, made on screen, that what is going on inside anybody is not visible from the far side of a road.

concept_links.why: The merge exists for this digest's third axis. The sources separate wanting that arises sharply, of its own nature [C006-P:L44], from wanting urged on by others or by one's own pushing of a hesitant mind [C006-M:L5] [C006-P:L58–L62], and note that the urged kind carries a sluggishness the spontaneous kind does not [C006-P:L62]; and they sort the same wanting again by gladness or flat feeling [C006-P:L25] [C006-P:L74]. Two roadside strips, one built on hailing and one on abundance, put one side of that axis on each — and the beat that follows the cut says outright that the lens cannot separate them, which is the digest's own position rather than a piece of modesty. The digest's limits are written into the sequence and not parked in the risks. The second axis, the justifying story, is chiefly about denying consequences [C006-P:L33], is flagged as sensitive and needing editorial care, and must never be mapped onto anyone's faith or read off a stranger through a windscreen, so beat 7 names it and refuses it. The Margaya's ranking of flat wanting above glad wanting [C006-M:L19] is recorded in the digest as having no commentarial basis in the extract and needing an expert check, so the same beat declines to state the weight. 'I was pushed into it' is not an excuse in these sources: prompted wanting is ranked weaker and is still wanting, which beat 5 says. The Pradeepika's background conditions for the spontaneous kind — temperament, health, patience, habit, company, suitable weather and food [C006-P:L46–L52] — describe tendencies and not fate and are not read onto anybody in frame. And the digest's warning that a host's generosity must not be confused with a guest's wanting is what the last beat is for: the arm held out over the road is not what is being classified.

This is the everyday sense-sphere world the count is a count of — sight, sound, smell, taste and touch offered at a car window [C004-P:L25] — with greed defined as the attaching that takes things to be good, beautiful or sweet [C004-M:L13], arriving with delight in one person and with flat routine in another [C004-M:L17], never with displeasure [C004-M:L15], and sometimes spontaneously and sometimes because somebody urged it [C004-M:L21], which is the same axis the primary concept sorts and is why this digest belongs in the merge rather than beside it. The digest's guard is the film's second beat and its whole posture: twenty-four of the fifty-four are counted beautiful [C004-P:L27], so these sources do not treat sense life as simply bad, and a film about two trading roads must not leave a viewer thinking a livelihood is a moral warning. The Pradeepika's own contemporary commentary on meat, gambling, drink and other faiths' views [C004-P:L55–L69] is that author's moral argument, is named by the digest as something that would wound if turned on people on screen, and is not carried here at all.

The dial the camera actually sees is feeling, and this digest is what keeps the film from reading it as evidence. Feeling is the tasting of an object's flavour, present in every mind because every mind takes an object [C032-P:L41] [C032-P:L43], experienced as pleasant, unpleasant or neither, with no fourth way [C032-M:L5]. The counts are what make beat 6 work: sixty-two minds carry gladness and fifty-five carry neutral feeling [C032-M:L9] [C032-M:L13], the joyful greed-rooted minds sit among the pleasant ones [C032-P:L58], and plain bodily pleasure has a single seat while the rest of the glad minds are mental gladness [C032-P:L99–L101] — which is why two faces can differ over one sealed packet at one price. Its guards travel with it. Neutral does not mean numb, since fifty-five minds carry neutral feeling including the most refined [C032-P:L75–L83]. Pleasant feeling is not the enemy, since it runs through generous and kind minds too, and the group's line that pleasant feeling is where wanting begins is named by the digest as an editorial compression that is not in these extracts, so it is never spoken. The Pradeepika's technical sense of all conditioned feeling as suffering [C032-P:L111] and its suffering of change [C032-P:L117] are not used here and must not be smuggled in as gloom over a season ending; the digest rules out 'life is suffering' as a mood. Its own wording for the neutral object [C032-P:L75] is flagged as possibly garbled and is not used.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the same reaching can arrive because somebody held something out or because nobody did, and that from outside the two are indistinguishable — which is worth knowing mostly about oneself. That being talked into something makes it weaker in these books' reckoning without making it anybody else's. That wanting also comes glowing or completely flat, that the flat kind is the one nobody recognises, and that neither temperature is the moral one. And that the gladness is not sitting in the thing, which anybody can test by watching two people buy the same sealed packet at the same stall for the same price.
what_must_be_real: The real trade of both roads, their real hours and seasons, and the real prices people pay, including the fact that most vehicles do not stop. Nobody is asked to hail a vehicle, to hesitate, to turn back, to taste, to refuse or to buy anything for the camera; no stall is dressed, no heap rebuilt and no exchange replayed. Prices are whatever is chalked up that afternoon. The two halves of the central cut are two real events filmed on two real roads and are never manufactured by staging either side of it. No seller is filmed in a way that would damage their trade; no buyer is followed or identified by their vehicle; no face is held at the moment money changes hands, and no shot is built to make anybody look acquisitive. No single person carries a point about appetite, and no single seller carries a point about persuasion. If a seller or a buyer does not want to be filmed they are not in the film, and the crew never stands where it puts anybody on a live carriageway.
position_hint: middle, early: the group's plainest anatomy of wanting and its fastest piece of cinema, best placed after a film has established what these sources mean by reaching and before the films that complicate it. It is also the group's explicit statement of what a camera cannot see, so everything after it can lean on that. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Making anybody in frame look greedy. A camera cannot show greed and these digests say so; nobody is filmed in order to be an example of appetite, no face is held at the moment of a transaction, and no shot is composed to read as an accusation. This is the group's hardest problem and it is a framing problem as much as a narration problem.
Mocking sellers or buyers, or letting the camera find roadside commerce and its customers funny. The digests name this as the one thing that would sink a film about a trading place.

Making the sellers' appearance the subject. Almost all published writing about the all-year strip is about how the women who sell there look, and a film that repeats that has made a different film — one about being looked at rather than about wanting. The camera's own position, on the far side of a carriageway with a long lens pointed at women who have to wave at strangers for a living, is part of what this film has to handle honestly and out loud.
Treating either trade as a moral condition. Livelihoods are not destinies, and these are people working for a living on the edge of live traffic.
Confusing the seller's holding-out with the buyer's reaching, which the C006 digest warns against explicitly. Only one of the two is being classified, and the last beat says so.

Reading the second dial, the justifying story, off a stranger at a car window. It is interior, the sources' examples are chiefly denials of consequence [C006-P:L33], and the digest forbids mapping it onto any community's faith.
Asserting the Margaya's ranking of flat wanting above glad wanting [C006-M:L19], which the digest records as having no commentarial basis in the extract and needing an expert check.
Letting 'they were talked into it' work as an excuse. Prompted wanting is ranked weaker in these sources and is not absolved by them.
Reading the Pradeepika's conditions for spontaneous wanting [C006-P:L46–L52] as fate or as genetics; the digest rules both out.
Turning flatness into a diagnosis. Neutral feeling is counted in fifty-five kinds of mind including the most refined [C032-P:L75–L83], so a flat face proves nothing on its own.
Presenting the group's line that pleasant feeling is where wanting begins as though these extracts said it. They do not, and the C032 digest names the compression.

Turning the end of the season into melancholy. The suffering of change [C032-P:L117] is a technical point about conditioned feeling, not a mood piece, and the film's ending is a cut and a noise, not an elegy.
Carrying the Pradeepika's own moral commentary on meat, gambling, drink and the rest into the film [C004-P:L55–L69]; it is that author's contemporary argument and not the taxonomy.
Ending on 'the sense world is a trap', which the count itself refuses: twenty-four of the fifty-four are the beautiful minds [C004-P:L27].

Consent obtained through a car window in a few seconds, at speed, in more than one language, from people who are about to drive away — and consent from sellers who have good reason to expect a camera to want something else.
Becoming a trade report. Yields, prices, expressway diversions and the economics of a glut are the film's human weight, not its subject.

The plain physical danger of working and filming at the edge of two busy roads, for sellers, buyers and crew; and drone permission over a national highway and over an inhabited valley, which the film should be prepared to do without entirely.
drop_if: The sellers on either road will not have a camera at the verge, or the film can only be made by standing where it puts people on a live carriageway.
Access can only be had on terms that require sellers to hail vehicles or customers to repeat a purchase for the camera.
The central cut cannot be obtained honestly — that is, if one of its two halves would have to be arranged.
The season fails, or the seasonal trade has been moved off the verge, so that the unhailed stop no longer happens in public.
Either trade can only be filmed as something arranged for visitors rather than as an ordinary day's selling.
The film cannot be made without turning the sellers' appearance into its subject.

connections.note: This film absorbed IDEA-0021 entirely: the seasonal fruit roadside is now the second of this film's two strips, and that record's research, verified sources, citations and risks are carried here. IDEA-0021 is now a different film at a different place and nothing in this record depends on it.
Things made because they will be wanted, and then the six seconds in which the wanting has to be produced in a stranger who was not going to stop.
Two kinds of buying: one where the seller calls to a stranger at speed, and one where the buyers call a price at a seller who is not in the room.
Two places where one object meets several different feelings at once, and the difference is not in the object.

selection.reason: Two near-duplicate candidates — produce sold at a verge to vehicles that had no intention of stopping — became one film by supplying opposite ends of the concept's spontaneous-or-prompted axis on two different roads, in two different seasons, with two different crops, so that the axis can be cut rather than asserted and the film can then admit that the camera cannot make the distinction it has just drawn. It also frees a record and gives the group its only film about speed and about the moment of exchange itself.

review.note: Rewritten as a merge, so the body is new and any older verdict no longer applies. This record absorbs the other candidate's film entirely — a river-valley road buried in fruit for eight weeks — and that record has been repurposed for a different film at a different place, so this is now the only place that material survives. The reason for merging is doctrinal and not tidiness. The primary concept sorts the greed-rooted minds on three axes, and one of them is spontaneous or prompted, asaṅkhārika or sasaṅkhārika: whether the state arises sharply of its own nature or has to be urged along, by somebody else or by one's own coaxing of a mind that is holding back. Kept apart, the two ideas were the same film twice — a road where produce is sold to people who were not going to stop — and each had to assert that axis with both of its sides happening a few metres apart on one verge. Put together they give the axis as a pair on the same kind of ground: at one strip an arm goes out and the vehicle stops because it was hailed, and at the other the road is so buried in fruit that vehicles slow with nobody signalling to them, and, as the absorbed idea's own logline said, from ten metres away there is no telling which is which. That clause is now the film: the shots are matched, the cut is the payoff, the viewer fails to sort them, and the voice says plainly that the texts' own marker for the urged kind — a heaviness the sharp kind does not have — is not something a lens can see. The three concepts and their roles are unchanged. The style is the group's fast film and shares nothing with its neighbours: six-second transactions, long lenses from across a carriageway, a shallow compressed plane, repetition, traffic noise throughout, two crops and two seasons, no aerial reveal and no golden-hour payoff. On the floor: a camera cannot show greed, no identifiable person is presented as greedy, grasping or calculating, no face is held at the moment of a transaction, no shot is built to make anybody look acquisitive, and the film states on screen that what is going on inside anybody is not visible. New title; both old titles are kept in aliases. A historical thread has been researched and added, and it is thin in one half and honest about it: the road itself is well documented, the all-year strip has a dated origin story resting on a single newspaper feature that contradicts other press accounts, and the seasonal roadside has effectively no documented origin at all. That is recorded as a gap rather than filled in. Images are no longer empty, but none of them is of either strip: they are the road in 1841, the memorial to the engineer who died building it, a seventeenth-century drawing of the fort at the second village, the two crops, and a roadside stall of the same kind photographed elsewhere in the country, each captioned as what it is.

suggested_location.region: Gampaha District, Western Province, for both strips, with the second running across the district boundary into Colombo District: the A1 trunk road about forty kilometres inland from Colombo between Nittambuwa and Pasyala, and the Kelani valley road from Biyagama through Malwana towards Hanwella, about fifteen kilometres north-east of Colombo
suggested_location.why_here: Two places whose entire economy is the production of a decision in strangers, at speed, in public, several hundred times a day — and which produce that decision by opposite means, which is the only reason they are in one film. On the trunk road the inducement is physical and visible: sellers step out from the verge and hold a packet up at windscreen height, and a vehicle stops because it was hailed. In the valley, for eight or nine weeks a year, the abundance does the work: the crop grows in back gardens and over lanes rather than in plantations, the trade has nowhere to happen but the verge of the through road, the road turns into a continuous red line, and vehicles slow with nobody signalling to them. That is the concept's spontaneous-and-prompted pair, supplied by two real places rather than asserted over one. The pairing also gives the film its central shot, which is a cut: the same lens, the same height and the same distance across the same width of tarmac, one stop of each kind, laid end to end so that a viewer cannot tell them apart. Both strips are strips rather than enclosures, which keeps the film out of the market-from-above image entirely; both put the whole transaction in public, in daylight, within a metre or two of moving traffic; and on both the refusals are the honest majority of the day, which stops the film pretending that wanting always ends in a sale. The trunk-road strip adds one thing the valley cannot: because the goods are identical, sealed and priced, two buyers at one stall differ in nothing but their faces, which is the feeling beat. The valley adds one thing the trunk road cannot: a season, with a beginning, a glut and an end, so the film has a second clock to cut against the first.

historical_thread.story:
The road under the first strip is the older and much the better documented of the two things in this film. It is the island's first modern highway, cut inland from the coast to the old Kandyan capital after the British annexation of the interior, and it is the reason there is any traffic on that verge to sell to. Construction began in 1820. The engineer in charge was Captain William Francis Dawson of the Royal Engineers, and Major Thomas Skinner is named alongside him in the standard accounts; the work is usually credited to the direction of Governor Sir Edward Barnes, though not every reference agrees on the governor. Rather than going round the great rock barrier at the head of the pass into the hills, the road was driven through it, and the rock tunnel of the 1820s survives, bypassed, above the modern carriageway; a Sinhala prophecy that foreigners could not rule the up-country unless they pierced the mountains is attached to the tunnel in popular retelling. Dawson died on 28 March 1829, before the work was finished, reportedly of a snakebite, and a memorial tower was put up for him at the head of the pass in 1832, the same year the first coach service ran on the finished road. The road is now numbered as the island's A1, runs a little under a hundred and sixteen kilometres from the fort in the capital to the hill capital, and forms part of an Asian Highway route. A lithograph published in 1851 after drawings made by the Russian traveller Alexei Saltykov in April 1841 is captioned simply 'Route entre Colombo et Kandy' and shows the road seventeen years after it opened: coconut palms, people walking, and a European riding in an elephant-drawn cart.

The cashew trade on that road is much younger than the road, and its origin story rests on one newspaper feature. A 2007 article in Arab News gives the trade a founder and two dates. In 1934, it says, a resident of the village named Johnna Hamee spread cashew nuts at the roadside, laid a large coconut leaf over them and set it alight to roast them, intending to sell them in the capital, and then discovered that she could sell them from a makeshift wayside stall where she stood. In 1946 her daughter Mai Nona, by then running the business, introduced the bright redda and hatte — the traditional Sinhala cloth and jacket in strong colours — as a way of attracting the attention of passing vehicles. The same article says that the village, formerly called Iddamalgoda, took the name of the trade, from cadju for the cashew and gama for village, and that the nuts are not grown on that road at all but brought in from Kurunegala and Alawwa, some thirty kilometres away. Other press accounts give the stretch a longer and vaguer past: a 2013 report in the Global Press Journal, which counted nearly a hundred women selling there daily and gave the village's other name as Bataleeya, says villagers have sold nuts there for generations and that the trade dates back at least to the early 1800s, when vendors sold to British colonisers; travel writing puts it at 'over a century', back to when the road was gravel and the traffic was horse carriages and bullock carts; and a Daily FT feature credits the place with more than two hundred years and says the stalls were revamped under the presidency of Ranasinghe Premadasa, whose village-reawakening programme ran through the 1980s and into the 1990s. Prices from the 2013 report — wholesale around two thousand rupees a kilogram, retail a hundred rupees for a packet of twenty to twenty-five nuts, and daily takings from nothing up to two thousand rupees — are the only figures found that were gathered at the verge.

The second strip's crop has a long history and its roadside trade has almost none. Rambutan is native to the Malay archipelago and is said to have been brought to the island by the Portuguese, who built a fort at Malwana on the banks of the Kelani in the 1590s, used it as a governor's residence, and abandoned it after Kandyan attacks in the 1630s; the Dutch occupied and probably rebuilt it, and the site was declared an archaeological protected monument on 24 July 2009. A drawing of the fort with its store and its church, made in 1662 and now in the Rijksmuseum, survives in the sketchbook of Esaias Boursse. The soil of the valley suited the tree, the village's name attached itself to the fruit, and the belt of orchards now runs from Biyagama up the river towards Hanwella with that village as its heartland; the trees flower around May and the fruit runs from June to the middle of August, a mature tree carrying something in the order of ten to fifteen thousand fruits. A 2007 Sunday Times report on the season records growers and traders by name and the practice of leasing a whole orchard for the season, one grower having leased two and a half acres for two months for six hundred thousand rupees. When the roadside selling of the fruit began, and where, is not recorded in anything this research could find. One retail account claims that street sales of the fruit began on the same trunk road as the cashew strip, close to the same town, and spread from there to the streets of the capital — which would make the two halves of this film descendants of one another — but the claim appears on a shopping site, is undated, carries no source, and was not found anywhere else. A photograph of about 1905, published as a colonial postcard, shows three women seated on the ground selling the fruit from baskets somewhere in the island; it establishes that the fruit was being sold by women at ground level a century ago, and nothing about a road.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
The concept's third axis is whether a state arises of its own nature or has to be induced, and the one dated fact in this whole record is the invention of an inducement. In 1946, on the evidence of a single newspaper feature, somebody running a roadside cashew stall worked out that a strong colour at the edge of a fast road makes vehicles stop, and put on the bright cloth and jacket deliberately, as a device. That is prompting with a date on it: not a metaphor for the sasaṅkhārika side of the axis but an actual technique, invented for an actual road, and still in use eighty years later. The other half of the film has no such moment and, as far as any source goes, never needed one — the fruit is simply there in quantities the valley cannot eat, and vehicles slow because the road has turned red. So the archive divides the same way the doctrine does: one side has a recorded act of inducement, the other has an abundance nobody had to invent.

The road binds the same axis a second way, from underneath. Every stop on either verge is made by somebody who was going somewhere else, and the reason they are going past at all is a piece of colonial engineering finished in the 1820s and 1830s for reasons that had nothing to do with either trade. The 1841 plate is the proof: the traffic in it is an elephant cart, and the road is already carrying people who are not from there. A livelihood grew on the condition of that traffic, the way the digest's background conditions — habit, company, health, weather, what there is to eat — sit under a state without determining it. The film does not read the road as anyone's fate, and the digest explicitly forbids it: those conditions describe tendencies, not destinies.

And the history binds the film's real subject, which is what cannot be seen. The strongest thing in this record is how little of it is settled. Four press accounts give the same hundred metres of verge four different ages — 1934, the early 1800s, over a century, over two hundred years — and every one of them is describing a trade that is photographed constantly and has never been written down properly. The seasonal roadside, which anyone who has driven that valley in June has seen, has no recorded origin at all. Two enormous, entirely public, entirely visible trades, and the record cannot say when either of them started. That is the same shape as the film's central claim: the thing is in plain sight and the question you want answered about it is not visible. The film says so out loud about a stranger's mind at a car window; the archive says it about the road.
what_is_certain: The trunk road under the first strip is the island's A1, running about 115.85 km from Colombo Fort to Kandy, classified as an A-grade trunk road under the Road Development Authority and forming part of Asian Highway AH43. Its route passes through Peliyagoda, Kelaniya, Kiribathgoda, Kadawatha, Yakkala, Nittambuwa, Pasyala, Ambepussa, Kegalle, the Kadugannawa pass and Peradeniya.

Construction of the Colombo–Kandy road began in 1820, after the British annexation of the Kandyan kingdom, and it is described in the standard references as the first modern highway in the island. Captain William Francis Dawson led the work and Major Thomas Skinner is named alongside him.

Dawson died on 28 March 1829, before the road was finished; the reported cause is a venomous snakebite. A memorial tower to him was erected at Kadugannawa in 1832 and was declared an archaeological protected monument on 6 July 2007.
The Kadugannawa rock tunnel dates from the 1820s work and survives, bypassed by a later upgrade of the highway.

A hand-coloured lithograph captioned 'Route entre Colombo et Kandy. Ceylan, Avril 1841', after the Russian traveller Alexei Dmitriyevich Saltykov and published in the second edition of his Voyages dans l'Inde in 1851, shows the road in use in April 1841.

Press coverage consistently places the cashew-selling strip on the A1 between Nittambuwa and Pasyala, roughly forty to forty-four kilometres from Colombo, and gives the village names Kajugama, Cadjugama and Bataleeya for it.

The Global Press Journal reported on 23 July 2013 that nearly a hundred women sold cashew nuts daily in the village; that the nuts are supplied by wholesalers; and that wholesale cost was about 2,000 rupees a kilogram, retail about 100 rupees for a packet of twenty to twenty-five nuts, with daily earnings ranging from nothing to about 2,000 rupees. Those figures are of 2013 and nothing more recent was found.

Press and travel accounts agree on the trade's visible method: sellers stand at the edge of the carriageway and hail passing vehicles from coconut-leaf huts and small fronts, and the goods are sold in sealed packets in raw, roasted and spiced forms.
Arab News reported in 2007 that the cashew nuts sold on that stretch are not grown there but brought from Kurunegala and Alawwa, about thirty kilometres away.

Malwana lies on the Kelani river in the Biyagama division of Gampaha District, about 14 to 15 km north-east of Colombo, at approximately 6°56′N 80°00′E, and is nationally associated with rambutan; a local variety carries the village's name.

A fort was built at Malwana by the Portuguese in the 1590s on the bank of the Kelani and used as a governor's residence; it was attacked by Kandyan forces in the 1630s and abandoned, later occupied by the Dutch, and the remnants were declared an archaeological protected monument on 24 July 2009.
A drawing titled 'Gezicht op het fort Malwana, met magazijn en kerk', dated 1662, is held by the Rijksmuseum as sheet NG-1996-6-84 in the sketchbook of Esaias Boursse.

Rambutan is native to the Malay archipelago. The Sunday Times reported in 2007 that the rambutan belt runs roughly from Biyagama to Hanwella with Malwana as its heartland; that the trees flower around May and fruit from June to about mid-August; and that a tree yields in the order of 10,000 to 15,000 fruits.

The same 2007 report records the leasing of standing orchards for the season, giving one case of two and a half acres leased for two months for 600,000 rupees, and farm-gate and retail prices of the day (about Rs 3.50 to the grower and Rs 6 to Rs 9 resold).
what_is_disputed: Most of this thread is thin, and the thinnest part of it is the one the film stands on. The origin of the cashew trade rests on a single 2007 newspaper feature in Arab News, which names Johnna Hamee as having roasted nuts at the roadside in 1934 under a burning coconut leaf, and her daughter Mai Nona as having introduced the bright redda and hatte in 1946 to attract passing vehicles, giving Mai Nona's age as 83 at the time of writing. No second source for either name or either date was found. The film treats this as one account, attributes it, and does not present it as established.

The age of the cashew strip is given four incompatible ways in the press: 1934 (Arab News, 2007); 'at least to the early 1800s, when vendors sold to British colonisers' (Global Press Journal, 2013); 'over a century', to when the road was gravel and travel was by horse carriage and bullock cart (travel writing); and 'over 200 years' with the colony 'established and revamped' under President Ranasinghe Premadasa (Daily FT). The early-1800s and 200-year claims sit awkwardly against the road's own construction dates. None was verified and none is used as fact.

The Daily FT article could not be read directly in this research — the site did not respond — so its claims are known only through search indexing, including a sentence dating the surviving original hut to seventy-two years after the first sale. That is recorded here as unread secondary material, not as a source.

Which governor ordered the Colombo–Kandy road. The Dawson Tower and Kadugannawa Pass references credit Sir Edward Barnes; the A1 highway reference credits Sir Robert Wilmot-Horton, who did not take office until 1831. The film names no governor on the strength of this disagreement, or names Barnes and says the attribution is contested.

When the road was finished. 1824, 1825 and 1832 all appear in the references consulted; 1832 is also given as the date of the memorial tower and of the first coach service, which may be the source of the confusion. The claim that this was the first coach service in Asia is repeated in popular writing and was not verified.

The prophecy attached to the Kadugannawa tunnel — that foreigners could not rule the up-country unless they pierced the mountains — is popular tradition. The reference that reports it notes there is no verifiable historical evidence for the interpretation.

That the Portuguese brought rambutan to the island, and that the fruit has 'more than 500 years' of history here. Both are reported as legend or as round figures in the press, the 500-year figure predating the Portuguese arrival of 1505 by a margin the sources do not explain, and no primary evidence for the introduction was found.

When and where roadside selling of rambutan began. This is the real gap. One retail site states that street sales of the fruit were first introduced on the Colombo–Kandy road close to Nittambuwa — the same stretch as the cashew strip — and spread from there into the capital. If true it would make the two halves of this film relatives, which is exactly why it is held here and not used: it is an undated, unsourced sentence on a shopping site and was found nowhere else. No history of the valley's roadside trade was located at all.

Whether the Premadasa-era village programmes built or rebuilt the stalls on the trunk-road strip. The connection is asserted in one press summary and nothing was found linking the Gam Udawa programme to that stretch specifically.

The effect of the new expressways on both trades. The Central Expressway is being built along the same corridor, and a trade that lives on through traffic is obviously exposed to it, but no source was found that measures the effect on either strip, and the film should not assert a decline it cannot document.

Everything about the two trades' own rhythm: the proportion of vehicles that stop, the hours the stalls keep, how the verge is divided between households, whether samples are offered, how the price actually moves across a season, and how many stalls there are now on either road. None of it is recorded anywhere found here and all of it is inferred.

what_to_film: The repeated unit, from a fixed long-lens position on the far side of the carriageway: arm out, windscreen, window, packet, note, gone. Filmed for whole hours on the trunk-road strip so that the rate and the refusals are real and not selected.

The same unit on the valley road in season, from the same distance, at the same height, on the same focal length. Matching the two set-ups precisely is the single most important technical decision in the film.
The unhailed stop: a vehicle that slows on the seasonal road with nobody signalling to it. The harder half of the central cut, and the one that cannot be arranged.
The hailed stop: somebody stepping out at the verge and a vehicle stopping because of it. The easier half, which must still be an ordinary one and not a demonstration.

A vehicle that passes the whole of the all-year strip, brakes a hundred metres on and reverses back along the shoulder. One unbroken take, a fixed camera and patience; it cannot be arranged and it is the film's fifth beat.

Two buyers at one stall in a single wide frame, one delighted and one flat, over the same sealed packet at the same chalked price — from far enough away that neither is identifiable and neither face is held.
The laying-out before six on the trunk road: shutters up, shelves set packet by packet under a bulb, against a road that is still only lorries.
A stall being built in the morning on the valley road from poles, wire and tarpaulin, and the heap going up on it.
The picking in the valley at tree height, for the abundance the second half of the argument rests on: hooked poles, limbs on ropes, sheets spread, sorting into crates at the foot of a garden wall.
The chalked price through the season, rewritten lower, and more fruit on a stall than there is traffic on the road.
The difference between an ordinary working weekday on the trunk road, when almost nothing stops, and a holiday afternoon, when the arms are out continuously.
Rain: both verges emptying in four minutes and filling again in ten.
Optional and brief, a flat overhead plan of a stretch of either road used as a diagram of braking, not as a reveal. The film is designed to work with no aerial footage at all.
The two endings: poles pulled out of the valley verge and stacked against a wall, and shutters coming down one after another on the trunk road.
Sound: the traffic, continuously, at its real level. There is no beat in this film over silence.
suggested_location.access: Both strips stand on the verge of public roads and the trade itself is public, so access is stall by stall and depends on the families who run them. The first is directly off the A1 trunk road about forty kilometres inland from the capital; the road authority and the police are worth approaching about anything filmed from the carriageway or the shoulder, and a long lens worked from the opposite verge is both the film's style and the safest position. The second runs along the Kelani valley road reached from the eastern suburbs of the capital, about twenty kilometres; its orchards are private back gardens and smallholdings and are entered household by household. Nothing is filmed from a position that obliges a seller, a buyer or a crew member to stand in live traffic or that puts anybody nearer the traffic than they already are. Flying over a national highway, and over an inhabited valley with a busy road under it, would each need their own permission; the film is built so that it does not need either.
suggested_location.best_time: The seasonal road fixes the schedule: roughly late May to the middle of August, heaviest through June and July, with the first and last weeks worth filming precisely because they are not the peak. The trunk-road strip can be filmed the whole year and wants at least two contrasting days — an ordinary working weekday and a weekend or holiday afternoon — which means the shoot is built as two blocks in season plus a return. Daylight and dry weather for both, since the trade happens standing outdoors on a shoulder; first light for the laying-out, the last two hours of light for the arms and the lamps and the shutters. Holiday weeks give the busiest version of the trunk-road trade and also the least consent-friendly one.

suggested_location.research_note:
Both strips are desk research only and neither has been visited. For the first: that this stretch of the A1 between the two named towns is given over to roadside cashew selling, that sellers step out from coconut-leaf huts and small block-and-tin fronts to hail passing vehicles, that the goods are sold in sealed packets raw, roasted and spiced, and that the nuts are brought in from about thirty kilometres away rather than grown there, come from the press and travel sources listed. The coordinates are an approximate point on the A1 between the two towns from an open gazetteer lookup, not a survey of the stall strip, and the elevation is a gazetteer figure for the area; the strip's exact extent has not been checked. For the second: the district's standing as the centre of the crop, the belt running from Biyagama towards Hanwella, the season from about May to mid-August with the heaviest weeks in June and July, the growing of the trees in back gardens rather than plantations and the seasonal stalls on the verge are from the sources listed; the secondary coordinates are the main village's as given by its own reference entry, not a surveyed point on the road.

The historical_thread block was assembled by web search on 25 September 2026 and none of it was checked on the ground or against printed editions. It is honestly thin in one half. The road is well documented and its dates are cross-read between three references, with the disagreements — which governor, which completion year — left standing in what_is_disputed rather than resolved. The cashew trade's origin story, including the two names and the two dates that make the film's best historical point, rests on one 2007 newspaper feature and no corroboration was found; it is attributed in the text every time it is used. The Daily FT feature, which is the source most often quoted for the '200 years' figure and for the surviving original hut, could not be retrieved at all — the site timed out repeatedly — so it is listed but was not read, and nothing is taken from it as fact. The seasonal roadside trade has no documented origin whatsoever: the one claim that would tie it to the same trunk road appears on a retail site with no date and no source and is recorded as an unverified claim rather than used. That gap is the honest answer and it is written into what_is_disputed rather than papered over.

Nothing about either trade's own rhythm has been observed: the proportion of vehicles that stop, the hours kept, how the verge is divided between households, whether samples are offered, how the price really moves across a season, current stall numbers, and what the new expressway corridor has done to through traffic are all inferred and must be checked on the ground. On images: Wikimedia Commons holds nothing at all of either strip, so none of the six references is of the location. Three are historical and belong to the thread — the road in 1841, the engineer's memorial far up the same road, and a 1662 drawing of the fort at the second village. Three are the object type — a cashew on the tree, rambutan in a garden in June, and a roadside fruit stall of the same kind photographed somewhere else in the country. Every caption says which it is, and every file was confirmed to exist through the Commons API before being written here. One caution belongs in the research and not only in the risks: almost all published writing about the first strip is about how the women who sell there look, which is a frame the film has to refuse and which will also shape how sellers expect to be treated by a camera.

unknowns: No seller, grower, trader, official or permission has been found or confirmed on either road. Everything here is a research direction.

Whether the central cut can be obtained honestly — an unhailed stop on one road and a hailed stop on the other, matched in lens, height and distance — is the single thing the film depends on and it has not been tested.
Whether the reversing vehicle, on which beat 5 depends, happens often enough to be filmed in a reasonable number of days is unknown.
The working hours, the proportion of vehicles that stop and how the verge is organised between households are unverified on both roads, and the film's rhythm is inferred rather than observed.
Whether the price actually falls across the season by anything like the amount assumed here has not been checked against real figures.
Whether either roadside trade can be filmed safely and unobtrusively from the opposite verge of a busy road has not been assessed.
Whether a drone can be flown over a national highway and over an inhabited valley, and on what terms, is unknown; the film is designed not to need one.
Whether sellers on the first strip will agree to be filmed at all, given how that place is usually photographed, is the first thing that would have to be found out.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is Claude's suggestion and awaits Chathura's verdict; its supporting detail is desk research and is unverified. No scene or shot is decided here.
